item.title: Can You Complete on a House Before Christmas
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

For many homebuyers, completing a property purchase before Christmas holds particular appeal. Moving into a new home before the festive season can bring both practical advantages and emotional rewards. However, whilst it's certainly possible to complete in time for Christmas, several factors influence whether this becomes achievable in individual cases.

The Challenges of Christmas Completion

The December property market often sees heightened activity as buyers aim to settle before the holidays. This seasonal surge can create bottlenecks in the conveyancing process. Homebuyers might face delays with:

  • Surveyor availability during the busy period
  • Local authority searches taking longer than usual
  • Solicitors handling increased workloads
  • Mortgage lenders processing higher volumes of applications
  • Chain complications if other parties have inflexible deadlines

Whilst estate agents and conveyancers typically work right up to Christmas Eve, unexpected delays can push completion dates into the new year. Borrowers might consider starting the process as early as possible in autumn to improve their chances of meeting a pre-Christmas deadline.

Speeding Up The Process

Homeowners hoping for a festive move may wish to explore ways to potentially accelerate their purchase:

  • Opting for a mortgage broker who can help identify lenders with faster processing times
  • Considering digital conveyancing services which may offer quicker turnaround
  • Requesting priority searches from the local authority (where available)
  • Being immediately responsive to all requests from solicitors and lenders
  • Choosing a property with no upward chain where possible

It's worth noting that cash buyers or those purchasing through auction typically have more control over completion dates. However, even in these cases, legal processes still require sufficient time.

Managing Expectations

Whilst a pre-Christmas completion remains possible, setting realistic expectations proves crucial. The average conveyancing process takes between 8-12 weeks, meaning purchases started in October have the best chance of completing before the holidays. However, each transaction remains unique, with some completing faster and others taking longer.

Borrowers might find it helpful to discuss timeline expectations with their solicitor early in the process. Some firms offer Christmas completion guarantees, though these usually come with specific conditions about when instructions are received and how promptly clients respond to queries.

For those who don't complete in time, there may be advantages to waiting until January when the market typically quietens down. Whatever the outcome, keeping communication open with all parties involved remains key to navigating the seasonal property market successfully.

item.title: How An Investment Platform Can Make Managed Investing More Accessible
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

For many savers, traditional savings accounts have long been a go-to option for stashing away money. However, with inflation often outpacing the interest rates offered by these accounts, they may not be the most effective way to grow wealth over time. Meanwhile, venturing into the stock market can feel intimidating, especially for those without prior investment experience. Historically, professional wealth management was reserved for individuals with significant capital, but thanks to digital advancements, managed investing has become more accessible than ever.

The Shift Towards Digital Investment Platforms

In recent years, digital investment platforms have emerged as a game-changer for everyday savers. These platforms leverage technology to provide access to institutional-grade investment strategies, previously only available to high-net-worth individuals. By automating processes and reducing overhead costs, they offer a more affordable and user-friendly alternative to traditional wealth management services. This shift has opened the door for a broader audience to explore managed investing, even with modest sums of money.

Benefits of Managed Investing Through Digital Platforms

Managed investment platforms come with several advantages that appeal to both novice and experienced investors. Here are some key benefits:

  • Accessibility: Many platforms have low minimum investment requirements, making it possible for individuals to start investing with smaller amounts of capital.
  • Expertise: Investors gain access to professional portfolio management, often tailored to their risk tolerance and financial goals.
  • Convenience: These platforms typically offer user-friendly interfaces and automated features, simplifying the investment process.
  • Cost Efficiency: By eliminating the need for in-person advisors, digital platforms often charge lower fees compared to traditional wealth management services.

For those looking to diversify their financial portfolio beyond standard savings accounts, managed investment platforms could be a worthwhile option to explore. They provide an opportunity to potentially achieve higher returns whilst mitigating some of the risks associated with direct stock market investments.

As with any financial decision, it is important to conduct thorough research and consider seeking independent advice to ensure the chosen platform aligns with individual financial goals and circumstances. Managed investing through digital platforms offers a modern solution for those seeking to grow their wealth in a structured and accessible way.

item.title: ‘Pain in the post’ for housing market as buyer demand weakens and mortgage costs jump
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The UK housing market showed signs of slowing momentum in September, as rising mortgage costs and economic pressures weighed on buyer confidence. According to the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (RICS), buyer enquiries declined for the first time since March, whilst agreed sales also softened. These findings highlight the challenges facing homeowners and prospective buyers amidst higher borrowing costs and uncertain market conditions.

Buyer demand weakens as affordability concerns grow

RICS reported a net balance of -22% for new buyer enquiries in September, down from -18% in August. This marks the first decline in six months, although it remains an improvement compared to the -41% recorded earlier in the year. Agreed sales also saw a slight dip, with the balance falling to -18% from -16% in August. Expectations for sales over the next three months also deteriorated, reflecting growing caution among buyers.

However, the latest Lloyds House Price Index paints a slightly different picture, with new buyer enquiries reportedly reaching their highest level since February. Whilst house prices remained flat in September, both monthly and annually, the average property price stood at £298,441. Prices also slipped by 0.2% on a quarterly basis, suggesting a cooling market.

Mortgage costs rise sharply, squeezing affordability

Higher mortgage rates have significantly increased the financial burden for borrowers. According to Moneyfacts, the average five-year fixed mortgage rate has climbed to 6.00%, compared to 4.91% at the start of 2026. For a typical £250,000 mortgage over 25 years, this translates to monthly repayments of around £1,611—an increase of £163 per month or £1,956 annually.

Rachel Springall, a finance expert at Moneyfactscompare.co.uk, noted that affordability remains a key challenge for buyers. “Higher mortgage rates and the rising cost of living are creating a painful affordability squeeze for new buyers,” she said. Whilst softer house prices might offer some relief, higher borrowing costs could offset any potential savings.

First-time buyers with larger deposits may find opportunities in a cooling market, but the overall affordability boost could be undermined by rising mortgage rates. Springall added that weaker demand might improve bargaining power for buyers, though this advantage could be limited by the broader financial pressures.

Despite these challenges, there are signs of more homes coming to the market, which could provide greater choice for buyers. However, the combination of higher mortgage costs and subdued demand suggests the housing market may face continued headwinds in the months ahead.

For those navigating the current landscape, staying informed about mortgage options and market trends could help in making well-considered decisions. Borrowers might also explore seeking independent financial advice to better understand their options in this evolving environment.

item.title: Agents hail Tory property tax shake-up – but warn ‘the detail will matter’
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Proposed changes to inheritance tax (IHT) and stamp duty by the Conservative Party have sparked mixed reactions from property professionals. Whilst many have welcomed the potential reforms, concerns have been raised about the finer details and how such measures might be funded.

Inheritance Tax Overhaul

The Conservatives have pledged to exempt family homes from inheritance tax, allowing couples to leave an additional £1m tax-free. Kemi Badenoch, during her keynote conference speech, even expressed an ambition to abolish IHT altogether, stating it would happen “as soon as we can afford it.” Estimates suggest these reforms could cost the Treasury approximately £6bn annually.

Timothy Douglas, head of policy and campaigns at Propertymark, described the commitment to remove IHT on family homes as a positive step for homeowners and families planning for the future. However, he emphasised that “the detail will matter,” warning against shifting the tax burden elsewhere. Douglas highlighted the importance of maintaining a stable and accessible housing market, particularly as households continue to face affordability and supply challenges.

Stamp Duty Reforms

Another key proposal is the abolition of stamp duty on primary homes, a move Douglas labelled as “significant.” Stamp duty has long been a major cost for those looking to move, and its removal could potentially stimulate the housing market. However, Douglas cautioned that any replacement tax would need to be carefully considered to avoid unintended consequences.

Trevor Abrahmsohn, managing director of Glentree International, was more enthusiastic about the proposals, describing the potential scrapping of stamp duty as “very welcome.” He argued that high stamp duty rates have historically held back the housing market, trapping capital in property that could otherwise circulate in the economy through retail spending and other activities.

Funding Concerns

Despite the positive reception, questions remain about how these tax cuts would be funded. Abrahmsohn voiced support for the measures but stressed the importance of ensuring they are “properly costed” to avoid unsettling bond markets. Similarly, Douglas urged ministers to collaborate with the property industry to ensure reforms support transactions rather than shifting the tax burden elsewhere.

Whilst the proposed reforms aim to alleviate financial pressures on homeowners and stimulate the housing market, their success will likely depend on careful planning and execution. As property professionals have highlighted, the devil is in the detail.

item.title: Comings & Goings
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The property market is seeing notable shifts in leadership roles, with Chestertons and Savills both announcing key promotions and appointments. These changes reflect the evolving demands of the property sector and the growing importance of specialised expertise in areas such as short lets and private client property management.

Chestertons Promotes Jordana Miles to Head of Short Lets

Chestertons has appointed Jordana Miles as its new head of short lets, a promotion that comes just under a year after she joined the agency as business development manager within the division. In her new role, Miles will oversee short-term lettings, which typically last between two-and-a-half to three months. She will work across Chestertons’ 35 London branches, collaborating with local sales and lettings teams to identify properties suitable for short-term tenancies.

Miles brings a wealth of experience to the role, having spent over five years at Draker Lettings prior to joining Chestertons in October 2025. Her background includes expertise in the short-let markets of Sloane Square, Notting Hill, and Fulham, as well as managing a team of eight negotiators at Draker’s Chelsea and Kensington branch.

Commenting on her appointment, Miles highlighted the benefits of short lets for property owners. “A property can still be well suited to the sales market even if it hasn’t found the right buyer yet,” she said. “Owners don’t necessarily have to leave it empty and absorb the costs while they wait. We can assess the demand for a short let, prepare the property, and generate income whilst keeping the sales strategy in view.”

Katinka Hill, head of lettings at Chestertons, praised Miles for her contributions to the team. “Jordana has been a driving force in our Short Lets team, combining real passion and focus with considerable expertise,” Hill said. “She has a clear grasp of what the service offers owners and occupants alike, and through close collaboration with colleagues across the business, she has made it easier than ever for clients to use this flexible option.”

Savills Appoints Adam De Acetis as Director in Property Management Division

Meanwhile, Savills has strengthened its Property Management division with the appointment of Adam De Acetis as a director. De Acetis will focus on expanding the division’s offerings for private clients, including property companies, private investors, family offices, and high-net-worth individuals.

With a background in property management, strategic asset management, lease advisory, and real estate development, De Acetis brings a wealth of experience to his new role. His previous work has included developing asset business plans, overseeing value-add initiatives, and collaborating with landlords and occupiers on portfolio strategies.

At Savills, De Acetis will work alongside the existing team to develop property and portfolio-level strategies for private clients. His appointment underscores Savills’ commitment to enhancing its services for high-net-worth individuals and private investors.

These appointments reflect the growing complexity of the property market, with both Chestertons and Savills investing in specialised talent to meet the needs of their clients. As the sector continues to evolve, such strategic hires could prove instrumental in navigating changes and capitalising on emerging opportunities.

item.title: Property professionals back homebuying reforms as industry calls for action
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

A recent industry poll has revealed strong support for proposed reforms to the UK homebuying process, with nearly eight in 10 property professionals expressing confidence in their potential to bring positive change. Conducted by Countrywide Surveying Services (CSS), the survey found that 77% of respondents were optimistic about the impact of these reforms, with 18% describing themselves as “very confident” and 59% as “somewhat confident”. Only 2% believed the changes would never materialise.

The Case for Upfront Information

The poll was conducted during a webinar exploring whether providing upfront property information could streamline the buying and selling process. Discussions centred on the benefits of making essential details available earlier in transactions, which could help reduce delays and improve certainty for all parties involved. Matthew Cumber, Managing Director at CSS, highlighted the importance of accessible, shareable information in driving meaningful reform. He emphasised that simply bringing existing checks and documents forward would not be enough; instead, ensuring useful information is available early in a standardised format could transform the process.

Collaboration Across the Industry

Cumber also stressed that successful reform would require collaboration across different sectors of the property industry. He noted that lenders, surveyors, conveyancers, estate agents, brokers, and technology providers must work together to improve the process as a whole, rather than focusing on individual components in isolation. By doing so, he believes the industry could reduce avoidable delays and provide buyers with greater clarity about the properties they are purchasing.

The webinar also touched on the recent appointment of Andy Burnham and its potential impact on the housing market. Opinions were divided, with 36% of attendees believing his appointment would make positive change more likely, while 16% thought it would hinder progress. Nearly half (48%) felt it would make no difference.

Looking Ahead

The discussion underscored a growing consensus that the homebuying process needs improvement, with attention now shifting towards implementation. As the industry seeks to turn ambition into action, homeowners, buyers, and sellers may wish to stay informed about potential changes that could affect their property transactions. With over 300 property professionals, including surveyors, mortgage brokers, and lenders, participating in the webinar, the momentum for reform appears to be building.

For those navigating the property market, keeping an eye on developments in this area could prove valuable, particularly as reforms aim to create a more efficient and transparent homebuying experience.

item.title: BTR investment so far in 2026 hits £4.2bn
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The Build-to-Rent (BTR) sector in the UK has seen significant growth in 2026, with a reported £4.2 billion invested so far this year. This surge highlights the increasing demand for rental properties, particularly in the single-family housing market, as investors continue to recognise the long-term potential of the BTR model.

The Rise of Build-to-Rent

The BTR sector has become a cornerstone of the UK property market, offering purpose-built rental homes designed to meet the needs of modern tenants. The £4.2 billion investment milestone underscores the sector’s resilience and attractiveness to both institutional and private investors. Single-family housing, in particular, has emerged as a key focus, catering to families and long-term renters seeking stability and quality accommodation.

This trend reflects broader shifts in housing preferences, with more individuals opting for rental solutions over homeownership due to affordability challenges and lifestyle flexibility. The BTR model provides tenants with professionally managed properties, often including amenities such as communal spaces, gyms, and concierge services, enhancing the overall rental experience.

What This Means for the Property Market

The influx of investment into the BTR sector is reshaping the UK property landscape. For landlords and investors, the growing demand for rental properties presents opportunities to diversify portfolios and achieve stable returns. Meanwhile, tenants benefit from increased choice and higher standards of living, as BTR developments often prioritise quality and tenant satisfaction.

For those considering property investment, the BTR sector’s strong performance in 2026 may serve as a compelling indicator of its potential. However, it’s essential to conduct thorough research and seek professional advice to ensure any investment aligns with individual financial goals and market conditions.

As the BTR sector continues to flourish, it could play a pivotal role in addressing the UK’s housing needs, offering a viable alternative to traditional homeownership and contributing to a more dynamic rental market.

item.title: More buildings need cladding remediation
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The issue of unsafe cladding on residential buildings continues to be a pressing concern across the UK, with thousands of properties still requiring remediation work. Despite some progress in addressing the problem, many homeowners and landlords face ongoing uncertainty regarding the safety and valuation of their properties.

Cladding Remediation Progress

Since the Grenfell Tower tragedy in 2017, significant efforts have been made to identify and remediate buildings with unsafe cladding. The government has introduced various funding schemes to support the removal of hazardous materials, particularly in high-rise buildings. However, the scale of the problem remains substantial, with thousands of residential properties still under scrutiny. Whilst some buildings have undergone remediation, the process is often lengthy and complex, leaving many homeowners in limbo.

Impact on Homeowners and Buyers

The presence of unsafe cladding can have far-reaching consequences for homeowners and prospective buyers. Properties with unresolved cladding issues may face difficulties in securing mortgages, as lenders often require evidence of remediation before approving loans. Additionally, homeowners might find their properties devalued or unsellable until the necessary work is completed. For those living in affected buildings, the uncertainty can lead to stress and financial strain.

Homeowners may wish to stay informed about their building’s cladding status and explore available support options. It could be worth contacting the building’s management company or local authority for updates on remediation plans. Borrowers considering purchasing a property in a high-rise building might also consider requesting detailed information about the cladding materials and any remediation work carried out.

Government Initiatives and Support

The government has introduced several initiatives to assist with cladding remediation, including the Building Safety Fund and the Cladding Safety Scheme. These programmes aim to provide financial support for the removal of unsafe cladding, particularly in buildings over 18 metres tall. However, concerns have been raised about the speed and efficiency of these schemes, with some homeowners reporting delays in accessing funding.

For those affected, it might be helpful to seek professional advice to navigate the complexities of cladding remediation. Mortgage brokers and financial advisers could provide guidance on how to manage the financial implications and explore potential solutions.

Whilst progress has been made, the cladding crisis remains a significant challenge for the UK property market. Continued efforts from the government, industry stakeholders, and homeowners will be crucial in resolving this issue and restoring confidence in the safety of residential buildings.

item.title: Landlord exodus could be offset by new generation of BTL investors, agent claims
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The UK rental market has seen a significant decline in available properties, with reports suggesting over 500 rental homes per day are leaving the sector in 2026. This trend has been attributed to increasing tax burdens, regulatory changes, and rising costs for landlords. However, amidst this exodus, there is speculation that a new wave of buy-to-let investors could emerge, driven by generational wealth transfers.

Inheritance Could Fuel New Buy-to-Let Investments

John Minnis Estate Agents suggests that the transfer of wealth between generations might provide a substantial boost to the rental market. Research from the Resolution Foundation indicates that 2.1 million adults received an inheritance between 2018 and 2020, up from 1.7 million in 2008-2010. Of these beneficiaries, approximately 32% inherited at least £50,000, equating to around 670,000 individuals. Whilst there is no direct evidence that these recipients will become landlords, even a small percentage investing in property could introduce a significant number of new entrants to the market.

The Shrinking Rental Market

Data from TwentyEA highlights the scale of the issue, with an estimated 111,696 rental properties sold by landlords in 2024, rising to around 181,000 in 2025. Since the start of the decade, approximately 834,800 homes have left the private rental sector. This reduction in supply has been exacerbated by mounting pressures on landlords, including stricter regulations and higher taxes. Against this backdrop, inherited wealth could play a crucial role in replenishing the pool of rental properties.

Wealth Transfers and Property Investment

Research cited by John Minnis Estate Agents reveals that not all landlords enter the market through deliberate investment. Around 40% of landlords initially purchased their property to live in or acquired it through inheritance or gifts. The remaining 60% bought specifically as an investment. John Minnis, founder of the agency, commented, “We’re entering a period where property wealth accumulated over decades is going to move between generations on a much greater scale. For those who already own their own home, receiving £50,000, £100,000, or more can create a completely different set of financial choices.”

Whilst inheritors may choose to reduce their mortgage, invest in stocks, or save the money, purchasing a rental property could also become an attractive option. Whether this potential influx of new landlords will offset the current decline remains to be seen, but it underscores the evolving dynamics of the UK property market.

item.title: Property Traitors: Zoopla cashes in on TV craze to reveal Britain’s secret movers
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Recent research from Zoopla has uncovered a fascinating trend among UK homeowners, with many taking secretive steps towards a potential move without informing those they live with. Dubbed “Property Traitors”, these individuals are quietly exploring the housing market, often without their partner or family’s knowledge. This behaviour sheds light on how homeowners are preparing for future moves, sometimes long before they officially announce their plans.

Secret Steps Towards Moving

The study reveals that 44% of homeowners have taken some form of covert action towards a possible move. This includes 27% who have secretly browsed property listings, whilst 21% have checked the value of their current home online. More surprisingly, one in 10 has gone as far as viewing a property without telling others in their household, and 2% have even made an offer in secret.

Among those considering a move in the next one to three years, the figures are even more striking. A significant 72% have taken at least one property-related action in secret, with 61% browsing listings and 36% researching new areas or towns. Nearly a quarter (23%) admit to having a “property crush” on a particular home, whilst 19% have saved or shortlisted a property. Even for those planning a move within the next 12 months, the trend continues, with 43% secretly browsing listings and 24% saving properties for later.

Where Are These Secret Searches Happening?

Many of these covert searches are taking place surprisingly close to home. Over a third (36%) of secret browsers have searched for properties whilst watching television with the very people they are keeping it from. Others have browsed at work or during their commute, whilst one in 10 waited until their partner was asleep. This suggests that many homeowners are conducting their property research in plain sight, often without raising suspicion.

Regionally, London leads the way in covert property activity, with 62% of Londoners surveyed admitting to taking property-related actions without informing their household. The West Midlands follows at 54%, whilst the North West records 53%. Scotland, on the other hand, has the lowest proportion of “Property Traitors”, at just 31%.

What Does This Mean for the Housing Market?

These findings highlight a potentially large pool of future movers who are already researching the market long before they make their intentions known. For estate agents, this could signify a significant opportunity to engage with prospective buyers early on. Homeowners may also wish to consider how their secret searches could shape their future plans, whether they are exploring new areas, calculating affordability, or simply dreaming of their next home.

Whilst the term “Property Traitors” adds a playful twist to the research, it underscores a broader trend of homeowners taking proactive, albeit discreet, steps towards their next move. Whether these secret searches lead to actual relocations remains to be seen, but they certainly paint a picture of a nation quietly preparing for change.

item.title: Professional landlord commitment remains strong
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Recent data from Fleet Mortgages indicates that professional landlords in the UK are demonstrating sustained commitment to the buy-to-let sector, with portfolio sizes growing and rental yields increasing, despite a modest slowdown in purchase activity during the third quarter of 2023. The findings suggest experienced investors are adopting a strategic, long-term approach to property investment despite current economic headwinds.

Portfolio expansion continues despite market challenges

The report reveals that professional landlords have continued to expand their property portfolios, with average holdings showing steady growth. This trend persists even as some investors adopt a more cautious stance towards new acquisitions in the current climate. Market analysts suggest this reflects a division between occasional investors and committed professionals who view property as a core component of their investment strategy.

Several factors may be contributing to this resilience among portfolio landlords. Many appear to be focusing on optimising their existing assets rather than chasing rapid expansion, with refurbishments and energy efficiency improvements becoming common strategies to enhance rental yields and property values.

Rental yields show positive movement

Fleet Mortgages' data indicates that average rental yields have continued their upward trajectory across most UK regions. This improvement comes as rental demand remains robust in many areas, while supply constraints in the private rental sector persist. Landlords with properties in regions exhibiting strong employment growth and limited housing stock are particularly benefiting from these conditions.

Property investors might note that yield performance varies considerably by location, with the North West and North East continuing to outperform many southern regions in terms of gross rental returns. However, specialists caution that yield calculations should always account for all associated costs, including mortgage payments, maintenance, and potential void periods.

The combination of growing portfolios and improving yields suggests professional landlords are successfully navigating the current landscape of higher interest rates and regulatory changes. Many appear to be leveraging their experience to identify opportunities where others see challenges, focusing on properties with strong fundamentals rather than speculative gains.

Strategic approach key to success

Industry observers note that successful landlords are increasingly adopting more sophisticated portfolio management techniques. This includes diversifying across property types and geographical areas, as well as carefully assessing financing options to maintain healthy cash flow. The professionalisation of the sector appears to be accelerating, with tax planning and energy efficiency considerations becoming integral to investment decisions.

While purchase activity may have softened slightly in Q3, experts suggest this could represent a tactical pause rather than any fundamental retreat from the market. Many established investors are reportedly reviewing their financing arrangements and waiting for the right opportunities, rather than withdrawing from the sector entirely.

For those considering buy-to-let investment, the latest figures reinforce the importance of thorough research, realistic financial projections and a long-term perspective. As the market continues to evolve, professional landlords seem to be demonstrating that experience and adaptability remain valuable assets in property investment.

item.title: Resi starts down 33% compared to last year
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

New data reveals a concerning downturn in residential construction across the UK, with housing starts plummeting by 33% compared to the same period last year. While private housing projects showed a slight quarterly improvement, the annual figures paint a worrying picture for the property market's supply pipeline.

Sharp annual decline in residential construction

Industry analysts at Glenigan have reported a substantial year-on-year contraction in residential construction activity. The 33% drop in housing starts suggests developers are facing significant headwinds, potentially including rising material costs, labour shortages and economic uncertainty. This decline comes despite government pledges to boost housebuilding, raising questions about whether housing targets can be met.

Private housing shows modest quarterly gains

The report does contain a glimmer of positivity, with private housing starts experiencing a small quarterly increase. However, this marginal improvement fails to offset the broader downward trend. Property market observers suggest that while some developers may be pushing ahead with projects, many others appear to be adopting a more cautious approach in the current economic climate.

The construction slowdown could have wider implications for the housing market. Prospective homeowners might find their options increasingly limited if fewer new properties enter the market, potentially maintaining upward pressure on prices. Those considering new build properties may wish to monitor market developments closely, while borrowers might find it valuable to explore how these trends could affect mortgage availability for new constructions.

item.title: Why More Landlords Are Looking at Refurbishment Projects – And How to Finance Them
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

In recent years, an increasing number of landlords have turned their attention to refurbishment projects as a way to expand their property portfolios. Whilst purchasing a ready-to-let home may seem like the simpler option, investing in properties that require renovation can offer unique opportunities. These projects allow landlords to improve a property’s condition, potentially increase its value, and secure higher rental yields. However, embarking on such ventures requires careful planning, budgeting, and an understanding of the financing options available.

The Appeal of Refurbishment Projects

Refurbishment projects have become an attractive option for landlords for several reasons. Firstly, properties in need of renovation are often available at a lower purchase price, providing an opportunity to acquire assets below market value. Secondly, by improving the property’s condition, landlords can enhance its appeal to tenants, potentially reducing void periods and increasing rental income. Additionally, refurbishing a property can lead to a significant boost in its market value, offering long-term capital growth.

However, these projects are not without challenges. Landlords must carefully assess the costs involved, including materials, labour, and potential unforeseen expenses. It’s also essential to ensure that renovations comply with safety and regulatory standards, particularly in areas such as gas, electrical systems, and energy efficiency. For those willing to invest the time and effort, refurbishment projects can be a rewarding strategy for growing a property portfolio.

Financing Options for Refurbishment Projects

When it comes to financing refurbishment projects, landlords have several options to consider. One common approach is to use a buy-to-let mortgage specifically designed for renovation purposes. These specialist mortgages often release funds in stages, allowing landlords to access capital as work progresses. Alternatively, landlords might consider a bridging loan, which provides short-term financing to cover the purchase and renovation costs before refinancing with a traditional mortgage.

Another option is to utilise personal savings or equity from existing properties. This can reduce reliance on external financing and minimise interest costs. However, landlords should ensure they maintain sufficient funds for emergencies or unexpected expenses. For larger projects, it could be worth exploring development finance, which offers higher loan amounts tailored to extensive refurbishments or conversions.

Whichever financing route is chosen, it’s crucial to compare lenders and seek professional advice to secure the most suitable deal. Understanding the terms, interest rates, and repayment schedules can help landlords make informed decisions and avoid potential financial pitfalls.

Key Considerations for Landlords

Before committing to a refurbishment project, landlords may wish to conduct thorough research and planning. This includes obtaining accurate cost estimates, creating a detailed timeline, and ensuring all necessary permissions are in place. Working with reliable contractors and tradespeople can also help streamline the renovation process and ensure high-quality results.

It’s also important to consider the target market for the property. Understanding tenant preferences and local demand can guide decisions about the type and scale of renovations. For example, energy-efficient upgrades or modern interiors may appeal to tenants seeking sustainable and comfortable living spaces.

Finally, landlords should factor in the potential impact of refurbishment on rental income and property value. Whilst the upfront costs can be significant, a well-executed renovation can deliver strong returns over time.

Refurbishment projects offer landlords a unique opportunity to enhance their property portfolios and achieve long-term financial goals. By carefully weighing the risks and rewards, and exploring the right financing options, landlords can successfully navigate these ventures and maximise their investment potential.

item.title: House prices flatline as ‘cheeky offers’ test seller expectations
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

UK house prices remained steady in September, with the average property value holding at £298,441, according to the latest Lloyds House Price Index. This follows a 0.3% decline in August and marks a year-on-year stagnation. Quarterly figures also showed a slight dip of 0.2%, reflecting a subdued market amidst rising mortgage rates and ongoing economic uncertainty. Despite these challenges, there are signs of renewed buyer interest, with new enquiries reaching their highest level since February.

Buyer demand shows tentative signs of recovery

Andrew Asaam, mortgages director at Lloyds, noted that whilst the market has been relatively quiet, property prices have demonstrated resilience despite higher mortgage rates. He explained that the Bank of England’s Base Rate changes have played a significant role in shaping market dynamics. “Higher mortgage rates and broader economic uncertainty are encouraging a more cautious approach from buyers,” Asaam said. “However, the increase in new enquiries suggests that demand remains steady, which could help sustain market activity in the coming months.”

Experts predict that house price movements are likely to remain modest in the near term, with any significant shifts dependent on broader economic developments. Amy Reynolds, head of sales at Richmond estate agency Antony Roberts, echoed this sentiment, stating that borrowing costs continue to be the primary constraint. “The market has lost momentum as we approach the final quarter of the year,” Reynolds said. “Annual price growth has slowed considerably, and mortgage approvals are noticeably lower than this time last year. Buyers are still active, but they’re being cautious.”

Buyers adapt strategies amid market uncertainty

Jeremy Leaf, a north London estate agent and former RICS residential chairman, highlighted how buyers are adjusting their strategies to navigate the current climate. “Buyers are testing seller expectations, ensuring that rising mortgage costs and inflation are balanced against market unpredictability,” Leaf explained. This has led to a rise in so-called ‘cheeky offers’, where buyers bid below asking prices to secure favourable deals.

Reynolds also pointed to the potential impact of the upcoming Budget on the property market. “For the remainder of the year, we anticipate prices to remain broadly flat,” she said. “Activity could pick up modestly if the Budget passes without significant surprises.”

Whilst the market faces challenges, the combination of resilient prices and improving buyer interest suggests a cautiously optimistic outlook. Homeowners and prospective buyers alike may wish to monitor economic developments closely as they navigate the evolving landscape.

item.title: Comings & Goings
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Two seasoned professionals in the UK property sector have recently taken on significant leadership roles, marking noteworthy developments in their respective careers. These appointments highlight the importance of experience and expertise in the ever-evolving property market.

Jonathan Hawthorne Promoted to Sales Director at Romans

Jonathan Hawthorne has been appointed as the new Sales Director at Romans, a prominent estate agency operating across the Thames Valley. This promotion comes after an impressive 25-year career with the company, during which Hawthorne has held various senior positions. Starting as a trainee sales advisor in 2001, he progressed to manage Romans’ flagship Bracknell office in 2014, later advancing to roles such as Area Sales Manager and Regional Sales Director.

In his new capacity, Hawthorne will oversee the sales operation across Romans’ 27 offices, ensuring the continued delivery of high-quality service to clients. Kevin Shaw, National Sales Managing Director at LRG, the parent company of Romans, praised Hawthorne’s leadership skills and dedication, stating that his deep understanding of the business and commitment to the brand make him an ideal candidate for the role. Hawthorne expressed his pride in taking on the position and emphasised his enthusiasm for collaborating with the agency’s talented teams to drive further success.

Charles Lloyd Joins UK Forbes Global Properties

Meanwhile, Charles Lloyd, a veteran in the prime residential property market, has joined UK Forbes Global Properties as a Founder Partner. With nearly four decades of experience, Lloyd brings a wealth of knowledge to his new role, where he will focus on serving clients across Prime Central London and the Home Counties.

Lloyd’s career includes notable tenures at Savills, where he established and led the Mayfair and St James’s operations, and CBRE, where he co-founded the Private Office division. He also ran his own business, Charles Lloyd Real Estate, before joining UK Forbes Global Properties. Martin Bikhit, Founder and CEO of the agency, highlighted Lloyd’s exceptional track record and longstanding relationships in the industry, underscoring the value he brings to the team.

These appointments reflect the importance of experience and innovation in the property sector, as both professionals look to leverage their expertise to drive growth and enhance client service in their new roles.

item.title: Chancellor urged to cut housing tax in move that could raise £4.2bn
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The Berkeley Group, one of the UK’s leading housebuilders, has called on the Chancellor to introduce significant changes to stamp duty in a bid to revitalise the housing market. The developer’s Budget submission highlights the sharp decline in new-build sales and proposes measures it claims could unlock 60,000 additional homes annually while boosting Treasury revenues by £4.2bn.

Proposed Stamp Duty Reforms

Berkeley’s proposals focus on reducing stamp duty for specific groups, particularly first-time buyers and downsizers purchasing new-build properties. The developer has suggested capping stamp duty at 1% for these buyers, arguing that such a move could stimulate demand and encourage more transactions. Additionally, Berkeley has called for the removal of the 5% surcharge on investors buying new-build rental homes, which could save a typical investor around £13,000.

The developer believes these changes could have a significant impact on the market. According to its estimates, removing the investor surcharge alone could increase sales by at least 30%, based on Office for Budget Responsibility figures. Whilst these projections are not independently verified by the Treasury, Berkeley asserts that a modest 7% rise in transactions would be sufficient to offset any lost stamp duty revenue.

Market Challenges and Potential Solutions

The housing market has faced considerable pressures in recent years, with higher mortgage rates, rising development costs, and broader economic uncertainty contributing to a slowdown. Berkeley has warned that the market risks “sliding over an economic cliff edge” without further intervention. In London, private new-build sales dropped by 56% in 2023 compared to the previous year, with just 8,840 homes sold in the capital.

Berkeley argues that reducing stamp duty could encourage both individual buyers and investors to re-enter the market. The developer also highlights the broader economic benefits of new housing, estimating that each new home generates approximately £49,800 in taxes and levies. Furthermore, encouraging older homeowners to downsize could create longer property chains, leading to additional transactions and revenue.

Rob Perrins, executive chairman of Berkeley Group, described stamp duty reform as “the best and quickest lever” to stimulate the housing market. He emphasised that such changes could have a positive ripple effect, benefiting not only buyers and developers but also the wider economy.

As the Chancellor prepares to deliver the upcoming Budget, homeowners, buyers, and investors may wish to monitor potential changes to stamp duty and their impact on the housing market. Whilst Berkeley’s proposals offer one perspective, any reforms would need to balance market stimulation with Treasury revenue considerations.

item.title: Pet project: New guide helps letting agents navigate rental rules
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

With renting laws across the UK evolving, tenants with pets are finding it easier to secure accommodation that welcomes their furry companions. Propertymark, a leading trade body, has introduced a comprehensive guide to assist letting agents and landlords in navigating the changing landscape of pet-related tenancy requests. This resource arrives amidst new legislation in England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland, each with its own set of rules regarding pets in rental properties.

Understanding the New Legislation

In England, the Renters’ Rights Act 2025 grants tenants the right to request permission to keep a pet. Landlords are required to consider these requests and cannot refuse them without reasonable grounds. Propertymark’s guide highlights the 28-day timeframe landlords have to respond to such requests and outlines valid reasons for refusal. Similarly, Scotland has introduced protections for tenants with pets through the Housing (Scotland) Act 2025, ensuring a fairer process for pet owners.

Given the differences in legislation across regions, Propertymark emphasises the importance of letting agents understanding the specific rules applicable to their area. This includes being aware of variations in permitted tenancy deposits and other local regulations.

Practical Steps for Agents and Landlords

Propertymark’s guide offers practical advice for agents and landlords handling pet requests. It recommends assessing whether a property is suitable for the proposed pet, considering factors such as size and type. Additionally, agents are urged to review leases and headleases for any restrictions before agreeing to a pet request.

Tenants can strengthen their case by providing supporting information, such as references from previous landlords or veterinarians, and even a “pet CV” detailing their pet’s behaviour and training. Propertymark also advises conducting detailed inventories and regular inspections to document the property’s condition, which can be invaluable if disputes arise over damage.

Benefits of Welcoming Pets

Contrary to common concerns, research suggests that pet-related damage is less than half the level of non-pet-related damage. Furthermore, tenants with pets often stay in properties longer, providing landlords with more stable tenancies. By discussing pets early in the tenancy process, landlords and agents can set clear expectations and foster positive relationships with tenants.

Henry Griffith, senior policy and campaigns officer at Propertymark, commented, “Pets are a significant consideration for many tenants, and handling pet requests effectively can greatly impact the tenancy experience. Our guide aims to provide property professionals with the tools to navigate these conversations confidently and consistently.”

As the regulatory landscape continues to evolve, Propertymark’s guide serves as an essential resource for letting agents and landlords, ensuring they remain informed and compliant while accommodating the growing number of tenants with pets.

item.title: Billionaire property tycoon quits UK as wealthy investors head overseas
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

David Reuben, the billionaire property tycoon, has become the latest high-profile figure to leave the UK, relocating to Monaco. Alongside his brother Simon, the pair share an estimated £28bn fortune and have long been prominent names in Britain’s property sector. Their portfolio includes significant commercial and residential assets both in London and overseas. While David Reuben’s spokesperson confirmed the move, no official reason has been given for his departure. However, it comes amidst growing concerns about the UK’s tax landscape following recent changes.

The tax changes driving relocation

David Reuben’s move follows the abolition of the UK’s non-domiciled tax regime in April 2025, which previously offered favourable tax treatment on certain overseas income and gains for qualifying residents. Monaco, where Simon Reuben has resided for years, is known for its tax-friendly policies, with no personal income tax, capital gains tax, or inheritance tax. Although David Reuben has not publicly linked his relocation to the UK’s tax changes, his departure aligns with a broader trend of wealthy individuals reconsidering their residency status.

Other prominent figures reportedly relocating overseas include steel magnate Lakshmi Mittal, hedge fund manager Chris Rokos, and BlueCrest Capital Management co-founder Michael Platt. Goldman Sachs executive Richard Gnodde has also reportedly moved to Italy. Changes to inheritance tax and capital gains tax have added to concerns, while speculation about potential tax increases in the upcoming Autumn Budget has created further uncertainty. According to the Sunday Times Rich List, one in six individuals or families featured two years ago no longer appeared in the 2026 rankings, with overseas relocation cited as a key factor.

Implications for the UK property market

The departure of wealthy residents could have a ripple effect on the UK property market, particularly in London’s prime and super-prime sectors. High-net-worth individuals and international buyers are significant drivers of demand for luxury homes, and changes to the non-dom regime have already introduced uncertainty. Some affluent property owners have reportedly been reassessing their UK holdings and residency arrangements in light of these developments.

For estate agents, further relocations could impact demand for high-value properties, though the extent of this effect remains to be seen. Much will depend on whether departing residents retain their UK properties or sell them. While the trend raises questions about the potential impact on investment, employment, and tax receipts, the long-term consequences for the property market are still uncertain.

As wealthy individuals increasingly explore alternative residency options, the UK’s tax policies and their implications for the property market will likely remain a topic of discussion. Homeowners considering their own financial and property arrangements may wish to stay informed about these developments and seek professional advice to navigate the evolving landscape.

item.title: Making Tax Digital Income Thresholds: Which Landlords Need to Comply?
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

HM Revenue & Customs' Making Tax Digital (MTD) initiative is transforming how landlords report their income, with phased rollouts affecting property investors at different thresholds. The scheme requires digital record-keeping and quarterly submissions through compatible software, but not all landlords need to comply immediately.

Current MTD Requirements for Property Investors

Since April 2023, landlords with combined property and self-employment income exceeding £50,000 annually must follow MTD rules. This threshold is calculated before expenses, meaning gross rental income from all properties determines eligibility. Those meeting this requirement should already be submitting quarterly updates through approved software alongside their annual tax return.

For landlords whose total qualifying income sits between £30,000 and £50,000, the compliance date is set for April 2025. This gives mid-range property investors additional time to prepare their systems and familiarise themselves with the digital submission process.

Exemptions and Special Cases

Landlords with property income below £30,000 annually remain outside MTD for now, though HMRC may review these thresholds in future. Some property owners might be surprised to learn that income from multiple properties combines towards the total - owning several modestly yielding properties could push investors over the threshold even if individual rentals generate modest returns.

Jointly owned properties require particular attention, as each owner must declare their share of the income. For example, spouses splitting rental income 50-50 would each need to assess whether their portion meets the relevant threshold. Trustees and non-resident landlords also face special considerations under the MTD framework.

Preparing for Digital Tax Reporting

Landlords approaching the thresholds may wish to consider several preparatory steps. Transitioning to digital accounting software well in advance can smooth the compliance process, allowing time to resolve any technical issues. Many providers now offer MTD-compatible solutions tailored to property businesses, some integrating directly with banking platforms.

Those affected might also review their record-keeping practices, as MTD requires maintaining digital records throughout the tax year rather than compiling information annually. Professional advice could prove valuable, particularly for landlords with complex portfolios or those who need clarification on how specific expenses should be recorded under the new system.

As HMRC continues expanding its digital tax initiative, staying informed about upcoming changes remains crucial for all property investors. While the current thresholds provide some landlords with additional time, the direction of travel suggests digital reporting will eventually become universal for tax purposes.
